subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 52-year-old man with central obesity and type 2 diabetes has a fasting triglyceride of 1240 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol of 96 mg/dL, and HDL cholesterol of 30 mg/dL; his HbA1c is 8.1%. He takes metformin and does not drink alcohol. Three weeks ago he had an episode of severe epigastric pain with a lipase of 900 U/L.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's hypertriglyceridemia?

options.text: Hepatic overproduction of VLDL related to insulin resistance
Deficiency of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein

explanation_correct: Insulin resistance increases hepatic fatty acid flux and VLDL secretion while reducing lipoprotein lipase-mediated clearance, so VLDL and triglycerides rise, the type IV pattern seen in type 2 diabetes and central obesity. Triglycerides above 1000 mg/dL predispose to acute pancreatitis, which explains this patient's episode of severe epigastric pain with an elevated lipase.

explanation_incorrect.A: Primary lipoprotein lipase deficiency (type I) causes chylomicronemia from childhood with a creamy supernatant and is not the pattern of adult-onset diabetes-associated hypertriglyceridemia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Apolipoprotein C-II deficiency also causes type I hyperchylomicronemia and would not present for the first time in a 52-year-old with the metabolic syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.C: Defective apolipoprotein E causes remnant accumulation (type III) with palmar xanthomas and combined hyperlipidemia rather than isolated VLDL excess.
explanation_incorrect.E: Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein deficiency causes abetalipoproteinemia with very low triglycerides, the opposite of the finding here.

educationalObjective: Type IV hypertriglyceridemia reflects hepatic overproduction of VLDL from insulin resistance and can cause acute pancreatitis when triglycerides exceed 1000 mg/dL.
